newsitem.title: UK: Halifax says UK house prices rise modestly in June.
newsitem.headline: Halifax says UK house prices rise modestly in June.

text.p: British house prices rose by a seasonally adjusted 0.3 percent in June, following a one percent rise in May, Halifax Plc said on Wednesday.
The Halifax house price index is now 7.1 percent higher than in June last year, up from 6.6 percent year-on-year in May.

Britain's newest bank and largest mortgage lender still forecasts house price inflation at seven percent in the fourth quarter of the year and is fervently hoping that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown does nothing to curtail the recovery in his first budget.
"The June figure supports our view that the housing market in general is continuing to recover slowly and not at the pace that some commentators would suggest," the Halifax said.
Latest figures on the number of housing transactions showed no growth between April and May and also indicated a subdued recovery, it said.
As a result, it made a plea to Britain's new Chancellor not to introduce measures to choke off the housing recovery on Wednesday, when he delivers the first Labour budget in nearly 20 years.
Brown is hotly tipped either to reduce or abolish tax relief on mortgage interest payments (MIRAS), or to raise stamp duty on house purchases.
The withdrawal of MIRAS would cost homeowners about 30 pounds each month. Stamp duty is currently levied at one percent on all properties purchased at a cost of more than 60,000 stg.
"There is no need for any specific budget measures aimed at curbing an allegedly 'booming' housing market," the Halifax said.

On Friday, the Nationwide Building Society, unveiled a more bullish housing survey. It said house prices rose 11.0 percent in the year to June, having jumped 1.5 percent in May -- the sharpest rise since March 1995.
Nonetheless it, like Halifax, said a harsh budget could stop the recovery in its tracks.
"The recovery, in its early stages in many parts of the country,could still be undermined," Paul Sanderson, Nationwide's head of research, said.
The apparent strength of prices belies a flat trend in transactions across the country, the Nationwide said. The strongest increases are still in London and the South East.

The Halifax index showed the average price of a new house was 72,450 pounds in June while first-time buyers paid 50,068 on average. The prices they paid fell by 0.6 percent last month but are still seven percent higher than a year ago.
